title: MYASTHENIC SYNDROME, CONGENITAL, 11, ASSOCIATED WITH ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTOR DEFICIENCY

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 (CMS11), which is associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency, is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding rapsyn (RAPSN; 601592) on chromosome 11p11.2.

checks.claim: Congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 (CMS11) is associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: Rapsyn mutations in humans cause endplate acetylcholine-receptor deficiency and myasthenic syndrome.
checks.explanation: Title links rapsyn-related myasthenic syndrome to AChR deficiency; CMS11 is OMIM nomenclature.

checks.evidence_quote: one patient carries L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3; two are homozygous for N88K; and one carries N88K and 553ins5
checks.explanation: Homozygous and compound heterozygous rapsyn mutations reported.

checks.claim: The RAPSN gene is located on chromosome 11p11.2.
checks.evidence_quote: RAPSN encodes rapsyn, a 43 kDa postsynaptic peripheral membrane protein that clusters the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the motor endplate.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature. The abstract does not state it, but it does name the gene.

paragraphs.text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 (CMS11) is an autosomal recessive disorder of neuromuscular transmission. It is caused by deficiency of rapsyn, which leads to endplate acetylcholine receptor (AChR) deficiency (Ohno et al., 2002). Engel et al. (2015) stated that most patients present in the first year of life and a few present later. Nearly one-third have arthrogryposis at birth, and intercurrent infections or fever can trigger respiratory crises. In Near-Eastern Jewish patients with a promoter mutation, the phenotype is milder, with ptosis, prognathism, facial and masticatory weakness, and hypernasal speech (Goldhammer et al., 1990; Engel et al., 2015).

checks.evidence_quote: we identify three recessive rapsyn mutations
checks.explanation: Recessive mutations causing a myasthenic syndrome (a disorder of neuromuscular transmission).

checks.evidence_quote: Rapsyn mutations in humans cause endplate acetylcholine-receptor deficiency and myasthenic syndrome.

checks.evidence_quote: Arthrogryposis at birth and other congenital malformations occur in nearly one-third of the patients.

checks.evidence_quote: Intercurrent infections or fever can trigger respiratory crises resulting in anoxic encephalopathy.

paragraphs.text: Goldhammer et al. (1990) described 14 Jewish patients from 10 families of Iraqi or Iranian origin who had congenital myasthenia with facial malformations. The malformations were an elongated face, mandibular prognathism with class III malocclusion, and a high-arched palate. Muscle weakness was mostly limited to ptosis, weakness of the facial and masticatory muscles, and fatigable speech. The course was mild and nonprogressive, and the patients responded to cholinesterase inhibitors. Antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor were absent. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz produced a decremental response, but a single nerve stimulus did not produce a repetitive compound muscle action potential.

paragraphs.text: Menold et al. (1998) studied 5 families of Iranian Jewish origin with 6 affected individuals who had been diagnosed with a phenotypically unique form of congenital myasthenic syndrome. Four of the families were consanguineous. Because all of the families came from the same geographic region, the authors considered it highly likely that they carried the same ancestral CMS mutation.

paragraphs.text: Burke et al. (2003) described 2 distinct phenotypes, early onset and late onset, in 16 unrelated patients with rapsyn-related congenital myasthenic syndrome. The early-onset form was often associated with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita and life-threatening crises. The late-onset form began in adolescence or adulthood and was at first mistaken for seronegative myasthenia gravis.

paragraphs.text: Das et al. (2014) reported a 20-month-old boy with rapsyn deficiency who presented at birth with weak cry, hypotonia, joint contractures, and facial deformity. Because of respiratory difficulty associated with muscle fatigue, he spent 71 days in the neonatal intensive care unit and 47 days in the pediatric intensive care unit. Imaging, metabolic tests, and electrodiagnostic studies were normal. Muscle biopsy showed myofiber atrophy in a pattern consistent with early denervation.

paragraphs.text: In 4 patients with CMS and endplate AChR deficiency, Ohno et al. (2002) identified 3 recessive mutations in the RAPSN gene. One patient was compound heterozygous for an L14P mutation in tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) 1 and an N88K mutation in TPR3. Two patients were homozygous for N88K. The fourth patient was compound heterozygous for N88K and a 5-bp insertion (553ins5) that causes a frameshift in TPR5. In HEK cell expression studies, none of the mutations hindered rapsyn self-association, but all diminished coclustering of AChR with rapsyn.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2003) determined that the major transcriptional start site of RAPSN lies 172 nucleotides upstream of the translational start site. In 1 patient with CMS (patient 1), they identified a -27C-G mutation in an E-box of the RAPSN promoter. The allele carrying this mutation was not transcribed in the patient's muscle. In 7 patients (patients 2 through 8), all of Oriental Jewish stock of Iraqi or Iranian origin, they identified a -38A-G mutation in another E-box of the promoter. Electrophoretic mobility shift and luciferase reporter assays showed that both mutations altered binding of components of myotube nuclear extracts and reduced reporter expression. The authors predicted that impaired transcriptional activity of the RAPSN promoter would reduce rapsyn expression and cause endplate AChR deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Engel et al. (2015) summarized that rapsyn concentrates and anchors AChR in the postsynaptic membrane and is required for development of the junctional folds. They described its domains: a myristoylated N-terminal region that links it to the membrane, 7 TPRs needed for self-aggregation and MuSK binding, a coiled-coil domain that interacts with AChR subunits, and a C-terminal domain that binds beta-dystroglycan. In rapsyn deficiency, multiple synaptic contacts appear on single muscle fibers. The endplate AChR deficiency is milder than in primary AChR deficiency, and the junctional folds are poorly differentiated. Different RAPSN mutations hinder rapsyn self-association or binding to AChR, impede agrin-MuSK-LRP4-mediated clustering of AChR, or decrease rapsyn expression.
